prize_parts.citation: For the development of halide perovskites as solution-processed photovoltaic absorbers and their realization in efficient solid-state solar cells

statement.case_for: My preferred configuration is unchanged: halide perovskite photovoltaics as a single part, credited to Miyasaka, Park and Snaith. The scientific case rests on a new, structurally well-defined and solution-processable crystalline family whose composition, dimensionality and defect tolerance can be tuned by design, and on a traceable chain of demonstrations: perovskite-sensitized cells (Miyasaka), the first durable solid-state devices (Park) and the mesosuperstructured and planar architectures (Snaith). Independent laboratories reproduced the efficiencies within a few years, and the field now has a large body of structural and spectroscopic work explaining why these materials behave as they do. In answer to the chair's question on what B024 adds beyond device engineering: it is the discovery that a defect-tolerant, easily processed semiconductor can reach silicon-class efficiency, which changed what materials chemists consider a viable photovoltaic absorber. That is a materials-class discovery, not a refinement of an existing device.
statement.case_against: The objections I raised in round 1 still stand and the first round did not answer them. Operational stability and lead toxicity are unresolved, much of the efficiency progress is device engineering, and Gratzel, Kanatzidis and Seok have strong claims that a three-person limit cannot accommodate. Kojima is not among the credited names. My configuration has no support from any other member, and I do not treat that as evidence for or against it. But it does mean the committee would be choosing between a still-maturing materials field and base editing, which six members include and which is the clearer majority-forming candidate. If perovskites are judged too early for deployment, I would accept B018 rather than defend B024 on its own against the committee.

responses.point: Chabes argues base editing is a clean chemical-biology invention, credited to Liu, Komor and Gaudelli, with reproduction in many laboratories and early clinical use, and notes the Kondo and Nishida priority question.
responses.response: Brzezinski's and your point that the adenine editor required evolving TadA to act on DNA moves me: that is a distinct inventive step and not the same idea realized twice, so a trio is more defensible than I allowed in round 1. I now rank B018 as my first alternative. I still want the Target-AID dates and the CRISPR 2020 distinction settled in the citation before I would put it ahead of B024. A citation that names the deamination of a base, and not RNA-guided cleavage, handles the second concern; the first has to come from the primary papers, and I cannot settle it from memory.

responses.point: Aqvist now proposes a two-part prize, Liu for base editing and Balasubramanian and Klenerman for sequencing by synthesis, as chemistry for rewriting and reading DNA, with a total of three laureates.
responses.response: I see the logic of the pairing and that it stays within three names, but I do not think a clean count of names makes the prize coherent. Both parts are tools for biology, and I worry the committee would be splitting the prize to reach agreement rather than stating one chemical idea. I am also unconvinced by the claim that sequencing credit is clean: Rothberg's 454 platform and Mayer's contribution are left out on the strength of one argument, that reversible-terminator chemistry is the core, which I accept as chemistry but not as the whole historical record. I would not move to this pairing.

responses.point: Somfai pairs Buchwald and Hartwig for Pd-catalysed C-N coupling with Liu for base editing, to give a synthetic-methodology half and a chemistry-of-life half, and acknowledges the 2010 prize and Kosugi as complications.
responses.response: We agree on Kosugi, and I still hold B054 as a strong alternative on maturity. But I do not see how your configuration answers the chair's question of what C-N coupling adds beyond the 2010 prize; ligand-controlled extension of an already recognized reaction family is a weaker novelty claim than a new materials class. Your own AGAINST section says the pairing may look like splitting the prize. I would also note that Buchwald and Hartwig together with Liu is three people, but that leaves no room for a trio on base editing, which is the very attribution question the committee is split on.

responses.point: Sparr makes biomolecular phase separation her entire prize, with Hyman, Brangwynne and Rosen as the core, and argues that about fifteen years of reproduction make the physical principle mature.
responses.response: I accept that the physical-chemical principle of multivalent phase separation is sound and widely reproduced in vitro. My concern is evidential, not about importance: which assemblies are liquid-like phases in living cells, and by what criteria, is still disputed, and a citation would have to avoid that claim. Your own point that Pappu and Mittag fall outside any three-name cut is a real weakness. By contrast, the perovskite claim can be tied to defined structures and independently measured device performance, which is the standard of evidence I apply to a prize.

responses.point: Linke, as chair, asks the committee to justify citing Balasubramanian and Klenerman for reversible-terminator chemistry alone given Sanger and Rothberg, and lists perovskites among his alternatives.
responses.response: I answered the equivalent question for B024 above: the citation is anchored on the first perovskite-sensitized and solid-state cells. For sequencing, I think the reversible-terminator argument is a legitimate chemical one and I do not doubt its impact or maturity. My difficulty is that a citation limited to that chemistry leaves the platform lineage to the cell of the prize that readers will see, and I would want that resolved before treating it as the safe choice.

uncertainties: Whether operational stability and lead toxicity make perovskite recognition premature, and whether the committee would accept the trio of Miyasaka, Park and Snaith without Gratzel, Kanatzidis and Seok
Whether Kojima's absence from the credited names changes the configuration
For base editing, the Target-AID dates versus the Liu cytosine editor and whether the adenine editor is a separate inventive step; I cannot settle either from memory
Whether the committee will prefer a mature, widely supported chemical-biology prize over a materials class still in development
statement.conflict_note: No conflict requiring recusal from any shortlisted ballot. My own field is electron crystallography of porous and nanocrystalline materials, which is adjacent to structural characterization of perovskites but I have no collaboration with the credited names, and I am a Stockholm University colleague of Peter Brzezinski, which does not bear on B024 or on any alternative.
